subject: Archaeology
title: The Archaeological Dig: How It Works
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Archaeological Dig: How It Works.

hook.text: Digging is the easy part. The hard part is recording every speck of dirt before it is gone forever.

buildup.text: Excavation is destructive — once a layer is removed, it can never be put back. Archaeologists call it 'unrepeatable.'

discovery.text: Sites are divided into square trenches using string grids. Every object is mapped in three dimensions before removal.

twist.text: Most archaeologists spend far more time writing notes, taking photos, and drawing plans than actually digging.

climax.text: Modern digs use total stations, drones, and photogrammetry — but the trowel and brush remain the core tools.

punchline.text: Digging destroys the evidence. The records are the real discovery.

quiz.question: Why is excavation considered 'unrepeatable'?
options: Government permits only allow one excavation per site
Once a layer is removed, it can never be put back — context is destroyed
Archaeological sites can only form once in geological history
